value: The main red grape, much of it from old vines on steep slate and schist slopes. Bierzo red wine must contain at least 85 percent Mencía, Garnacha Tintorera, Estaladiña or Merenzao between them.
source_notes: Appellation rules: red wine at least 85% Mencía, Garnacha Tintorera, Estaladiña and/or Merenzao; old vineyards mostly Mencía; average vine age around 75 years. World of Fine Wine: Mencía planted on slate and schist hills, old bush vines, Consejo claims highest concentration of centenary vines. GuildSomm: Mencía the most planted grape in Bierzo by a long way.

value: Here it is at its freshest and most lively from the high slate slopes, with red and black fruit and violet aromas.
source_notes: Appellation rules: vineyards up to over 1000 m make very fresh, lively wines; reds show red and/or black fruit and violet flowers, fresh with structure. World of Fine Wine: higher altitude Corullón wines straight and lively; slate sites give tense, mineral wines; floral wines with red fruit. Note: GuildSomm calls Bierzo Mencía more muscular than Ribeira Sacra, so this is the high site style, not every Bierzo.

value: The main grape of the white Txakoli, the most widespread style, made with Hondarrabi Zuri Zerratia, the other principal white variety. Authorised grapes such as Folle Blanche are capped at 20 percent of the area a winery uses for the white wine.
source_notes: Appellation rules (consolidated text published by the Basque Government): Hondarrabi Zuri, Hondarrabi Beltza and Hondarrabi Zuri Zerratia are the recommended or principal varieties; authorised varieties together and Mune Mahatsa (Folle Blanche) each limited to 20% of the area processed per winery for white wine. Consejo Regulador site: Hondarrabi Zuri is the main coastal variety; white txakoli, the most widespread style, made mainly from Hondarrabi Zuri and Zerratia. Caution: both trace back to the DO itself, not two independent organisations.

value: The leading grape, making up most of the vineyard; the appellation rules reserve the Calatayud Superior label for reds with at least 85 percent Garnacha from vines over 50 years old.
source_notes: Calatayud appellation rules (Aragón government): Calatayud Superior needs at least 85 percent garnacha tinta from vineyards over 50 years old, low yields. Decanter guide: Superior classification for at least 85 percent old vine Garnacha over 50 years. Decanter (Aragón): Garnacha makes up 70 percent of production in Calatayud. BBR (merchant): signature grape, over 60 percent of the vineyards.

value: From old vines in high, stony vineyards it gives concentrated wines that keep their freshness and show a mineral trace.
source_notes: Calatayud appellation rules: vineyards mostly between 650 and 900 m; older vines on stony and slate soils give more structured reds; wines concentrated with traits of minerality, balance of alcohol and acidity. Decanter review of one old vine Garnacha (single wine, lower tier): concentrated from very low yields with plenty of freshness. BBR (merchant): quality vineyards at 400 to 900 m.

value: A secondary red grape allowed by the appellation rules, used alongside Garnacha.
source_notes: Calatayud appellation rules: Tempranillo listed among authorised red varieties after Garnacha tinta. BBR (merchant, lower tier): Garnacha supplemented by Tempranillo and Mazuela.

value: The leading grape, making up most of the vineyard, much of it from old vines.
source_notes: DO Campo de Borja: The Empire of Garnacha; over 2,000 of its Garnacha hectares are 30 to 50 years old. Decanter (Aragón): Garnacha makes up 60 percent of production in Campo de Borja. The Buyer: Garnacha 60 percent of plantings; old vine focus. Decanter guide: self proclaimed Empire of Garnacha.

value: Its wines here range from warm and powerful in the low vineyards to finer and more elegant, with some minerality, in the high vineyards towards the Moncayo.
source_notes: DO Campo de Borja: low area wines warm, powerful, very aromatic; high area (Moncayo foothills, Tabuenca etc.) wines fine, subtle and elegant. Decanter guide: fleshy single varietal wines with some minerality from high altitude areas like Tabuenca.

value: The most planted grape in Cava and the most common one in its blends.
source_notes: Decanter: Macabeo is the most common variety in the Cava blend and the most planted in the DO. Wine Folly: the main grape in Cava, with the most vineyard plantings.

value: One of the three traditional Cava grapes, it usually plays a supporting part, adding delicacy to the blend, and does best in higher, cooler vineyards.
source_notes: Decanter: often plays a supporting role; elegance, delicacy and finesse; altitudes of 300 m and above unlock its potential (Llopart). Wine Folly: softens and balances the blend, delicate citrus and white flower notes. Guía Peñín: traditional variety of Upper Penedès, better adapted to cooler areas. Jeroboams (merchant): best sites at high elevations.

value: One of the three traditional Cava grapes, it brings acidity and structure and is often the main grape in the longest aged Cavas.
source_notes: Decanter: low pH and fresh acidity good for long ageing; for most of the longest aged Cavas Xarel.lo is the main component if not the whole blend. Wine Folly: adds aroma and structure, zingy acidity boosts ageing potential. Jeroboams (merchant): Cavas destined for long ageing have a high proportion of Xarel lo. GuildSomm: Macabeo, Parellada and Xarel·lo are the three primary grapes.

value: In Cava it adds a fennel scent and a firm, fresh line of acidity to the blend.
source_notes: Decanter (Cava grapes): flavour reminiscent of dried camomile and fennel with a bitter tone on the finish; fresh acidity. Jeroboams (merchant, lower tier): fennel scented Xarel lo supports Macabeo in Cava. Decanter Jefford tasting notes: fennel among the classic Catalan notes. Wine Folly: zingy acidity.

value: Listed in the appellation rules as Listán Blanco de Canarias, it is the most widely planted grape of the islands and the base of their dry whites.
source_notes: DOP Islas Canarias (canarywine.com variety page and appellation rules): Listán Blanco is the most widely planted grape variety in the Canary Islands, the same as Palomino Fino of Jerez; listed as Listán Blanco de Canarias. VinePair (lower tier): very important to dry white wine production in the Canary Islands.

value: One of the three grapes the appellation rules allow, with Palomino and Moscatel; its late picked grapes are dried in the sun for the sweet Pedro Ximénez wine, and it sweetens blends such as cream sherry.
source_notes: Sherry.wine (Consejo Regulador): regulations allow Palomino, Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel; PX grapes generally sunned before vinification to concentrate sugar, giving sweet wines. Decanter (pairing guide): PX grapes picked late and sun dried; cream sherry is roughly 75 percent oloroso and 25 percent PX.

value: In Jerez it makes a viscous, syrupy dessert wine, velvety in the mouth, aged only in contact with air.
source_notes: Sherry.wine (Consejo Regulador): velvety and syrupy in the mouth, with acidity to temper the sweetness; ageing exclusively oxidative. Wine Spectator: PX dessert bottlings are the richest and sweetest, often viscous and heady in feel.

value: The principal grape in the appellation rules and most of the vineyard; a wine labelled Jumilla Monastrell must hold at least 85 percent, and it also makes rosé and a sweet fortified red.
source_notes: Appellation rules (MAPA): Monastrell is the principal variety, more than 70 percent of the vineyard; Jumilla Monastrell needs at least 85 percent; rosés and fortified Tinto Monastrell made from it. Decanter (sponsored feature, likely tied to the DO): almost three quarters of the vineyard; bottled alone or blended with Cabernet Sauvignon or Syrah. The Wine Society (own label product page): native to the region, makes up most of the producer's vineyards.

value: In Jumilla it gives broad, fleshy reds with ripe fruit, generous alcohol and smooth, well integrated tannins.
source_notes: Appellation rules (MAPA): reds broad, fleshy, good alcohol, ripe fruit character, well integrated astringency; robust and fruity. Decanter (sponsored feature): balance, flesh, abundant silky tannins, plum and black cherry. Weak because the Decanter piece is sponsored and may not be independent of the DO.

value: The dominant white grape and the most produced variety of the appellation.
source_notes: GuildSomm: in Monterrei Godello leads total production. Cellar Tours (lower tier): Godello is the dominant white, the large majority of white grapes harvested.

value: Here it gives light, fresh reds with bright red fruit.
source_notes: Guía Peñín: young Monterrei reds have good fruit with herbaceous notes, light and fruity in the mouth. Cellar Tours (lower tier): Monterrei Mencía floral and elegant with bright, crunchy red fruit, compared to Pinot Noir.

value: With Garnacha, it is one of the two traditional red grapes that together make up most of the vineyard.
source_notes: DO Montsant: Garnatxa negra and Carinyena are the historic predominant black varieties, more than 65 percent of the vineyard. Club Oenologique: Cariñena and Garnacha, about 68 percent of vineyard space; Garnacha and Cariñena dominate as in Priorat.

value: With Cariñena, it is one of the two traditional red grapes that together make up most of the vineyard, and it is also the base of the traditional sweet wines.
source_notes: DO Montsant: Garnatxa negra and Carinyena make up more than 65 percent of the vineyard; Garnatxa used for generous (fortified) wines for its high sugar. Club Oenologique: Cariñena and Garnacha cover about 68 percent of the vineyard. Guía Peñín: reds can rely almost exclusively on Garnacha; traditional sweet liqueur wines are mainly Garnacha based.

value: Navarra's traditional grape and once almost its whole vineyard, it is the grape behind the rosados the region has long been known for.
source_notes: DO Navarra: almost 90 percent of the vineyard at the end of the 1970s. Decanter profile: about 90 percent of vines in the early 1980s, mostly for rosé; Garnacha rosé famous for centuries. Appellation rules: Garnacha gives the traditional rosados; 'Rosado Tradición' is 100 percent Garnacha Tinta. Decanter: the grape with the longest tradition in Navarra.

value: Promoted from the 1980s, it overtook Garnacha to become Navarra's most planted red grape, used on its own and in blends with Cabernet Sauvignon, Garnacha or Merlot.
source_notes: DO Navarra: great development in recent decades, becoming the majority red variety; young single variety wines and blends for ageing. Decanter profile: from the 1980s Evena promoted Tempranillo or a blend of Tempranillo with Cabernet Sauvignon, Garnacha or Merlot; Tempranillo now the largest share of plantings.

value: Grown mainly in central Penedès, it adds fresh acidity to white blends, and much of it goes into sparkling wine.
source_notes: DO Penedès (sponsored content on Decanter): Macabeu grown mainly in Penedès Central, used to add bright acidity to white blends. Guía Peñín: core variety of Central Penedès, where much production goes to cava. Jeroboams (merchant): mainstay of sparkling wine production, good acidity.

value: The region's flagship grape, used for fresh and barrel fermented still whites as well as for sparkling wines.
source_notes: DO Penedès (sponsored content on Decanter, two articles): flagship variety, most planted, produces vibrant whites, age worthy and skin fermented wines and sparkling wines. Guía Peñín: key traditional variety used in classic fruity whites and barrel fermented single varietals. GuildSomm: Clàssic Penedès sparkling mostly a blend of Xarel·lo, Parellada and Macabeu.

value: Here it often shows a wild fennel note alongside its fruit and herbs.
source_notes: DO Penedès (sponsored content on Decanter): contributes fruity and herbal character; a quintessentially Xarello wild fennel note. Decanter Jefford tasting notes on Penedès Cavas: citrus peel, fennel and dried wild flowers as classic Catalan notes. Jeroboams (merchant, lower tier): fennel scented Xarel lo.

value: A permitted red variety in the appellation rules, used in blends alongside Garnacha and Cariñena.
source_notes: DOQ Priorat: Cabernet Sauvignon listed among permitted red varietals; Garnacha and Cariñena are the recommended ones. Wine Folly: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah appear in smaller amounts in blends with Garnacha and Cariñena. Wine Spectator: vineyards feature old vine Garnacha and Cariñena along with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah.

value: From old vines on the llicorella slate it gives intense wines with a stony, mineral character, while young vines here seldom give expressive wine.
source_notes: Decanter (Stephen Brook): most century old vines are Cariñena; Cariñena needs to be at least 15 years old before it can become expressive; llicorella gives minerality. Wine Folly: young Cariñena vineyards rarely produce high quality wine; black stone minerality of Priorat reds. Jeroboams (merchant, lower tier): garrigue scented reds with cranberry and liquorice. Minerality is described for Priorat reds generally.

value: On the llicorella slate it gives powerful, high alcohol wines that still keep a fresh acidity and a stony, mineral character.
source_notes: Decanter (Stephen Brook): alcohol up to 15.5 percent especially for Garnacha based wines, rarely heavy thanks to enlivening acidity; llicorella stamps its personality on the wines, minerality. Wine Folly: black stone or hard rock minerality tied to llicorella slate. Jeroboams (merchant, lower tier): old vine Garnacha concentrated with balanced freshness and acidity. Decanter profile: once known for full bodied strength from Grenache and Carignan, now fresher. Note: sources describe Priorat reds as a whole, led by Garnacha and Cariñena.

value: A permitted red variety in the appellation rules, used in blends alongside Garnacha and Cariñena.
source_notes: DOQ Priorat: Merlot listed among permitted red varietals; Garnacha and Cariñena are the recommended ones. Wine Folly: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah appear in smaller amounts in blends with Garnacha and Cariñena. Wine Spectator: vineyards feature old vine Garnacha and Cariñena along with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah.

value: A permitted red variety in the appellation rules, used in blends alongside Garnacha and Cariñena.
source_notes: DOQ Priorat: Syrah listed among permitted red varietals; Garnacha and Cariñena are the recommended ones. Wine Folly: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah appear in smaller amounts in blends with Garnacha and Cariñena. Wine Spectator: vineyards feature old vine Garnacha and Cariñena along with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah.

value: The main red grape: Ribeira Sacra red wine must contain at least 70 percent Mencía.
source_notes: Appellation rules (DOG 18 Feb 2025, hosted by the Consejo Regulador): Ribeira Sacra reds at least 70% Mencía; Mencía the majority and fundamental variety of the reds. GuildSomm: Mencía is the region best known wine. Guía Peñín: Mencía the most characteristic variety of the region.

value: Here it is usually aromatic and light in structure, lighter than the Mencía of Bierzo.
source_notes: GuildSomm: Ribeira Sacra Mencía lighter, greener and more aromatic, Bierzo more muscular. Guía Peñín: aromatic and balsamic, dry, fruity and without a marked structure, with marked minerality. Counterview: Vinous calls Amandi Mencía ripe and compact.

value: The most planted and most characteristic grape, leading the white blends, usually alongside Torrontés, Lado, Loureira, Godello or Albariño.
source_notes: Appellation rules: Treixadura is the most cultivated and representative variety of the area, also the lead variety for the sparkling and Tostado wines. Guía Peñín: treixadura and torrontés the main native varieties, often joined by lado, loureiro and godello. Jeroboams (merchant, lower tier): often blended with Albariño.

value: The principal red grape; the appellation rules require at least 75 percent of it in red Ribera del Duero.
source_notes: Appellation rules (section 3c and 6): red wines at least 75 percent Tempranillo, Tinto Fino or Tinta del País, named the principal red variety. Decanter: 'the DO states that Tempranillo must provide at least 75% of any blend'.

value: Garnacha
source_notes: Appellation rules list it as 'Garnacha tinta'; riojawine.com (Consejo Regulador) and The Wine Society both call it Garnacha.

value: It has lost ground to Tempranillo and is now at its strongest in the warmer east, Rioja Oriental.
source_notes: riojawine.com: Garnacha has 'lost ground to the Tempranillo variety' and 'stands out in eastern Rioja'. The Wine Society: Garnacha thrives in Rioja Oriental, the warmer eastern zone. Decanter: Garnacha was once Rioja's most planted variety.

value: The backbone of red Rioja and planted in most of its vineyard, usually blended with Garnacha, Graciano or Mazuelo.
source_notes: riojawine.com: Tempranillo 'occupies most of our plantation' and is the core red variety. The Wine Society: 'Tempranillo remains the backbone of Rioja', crianza is mostly Tempranillo with some Garnacha. Appellation rules: reds at least 95 percent from Tempranillo, Garnacha Tinta, Graciano, Mazuelo and Maturana Tinta.

value: Grown here since the 1950s and mostly blended with Verdejo, where it lightens the body and adds acidity.
source_notes: DO Rueda: Viura began to be grown in the 1950s and is used in white wines for more lightness and a touch of acidity. SevenFifty Daily: cultivated in Rueda since the 1950s; blended with Verdejo it lightens the body and boosts acidity.

value: Planted here from the 1930s for the old fortified wines, it is still allowed for the Dorado and Pálido styles, but no new plantings are permitted.
source_notes: Appellation rules: Dorado and Pálido from Palomino Fino and/or Verdejo; no new plantings of Palomino Fino admitted. DO Rueda: planted from the 1930s, origin of the flor fortified wines. SevenFifty Daily: cultivated since the 1930s for fortified wines, new plantings forbidden. Decanter: Dorado and Pálido from Palomino and/or Verdejo.

value: Brought in during the region's revival in the 1970s, it is made on its own or blended with Verdejo.
source_notes: Decanter: Sauvignon Blanc is a relative newcomer, planted in the early days of the revitalisation (led by Marqués de Riscal), permitted as a single variety and in a blend with Verdejo. SevenFifty Daily: introduced by Marqués de Riscal in the 1970s; blended with Verdejo.

value: Rueda's principal grape and by far its most planted, made mostly into single variety whites and also used, with Palomino, for the fortified Dorado and Pálido.
source_notes: Appellation rules: Verdejo is the principal variety and the 'razón de ser' of Rueda; Dorado and Pálido from Palomino Fino and/or Verdejo. Decanter: Verdejo is the most widely planted (about 85 percent), Rueda's star grape; Dorado and Pálido from Palomino and/or Verdejo. SevenFifty Daily: most widely planted grape in Rueda.

value: In Rueda it makes fresh, lively whites with a distinctly herbal, grassy scent.
source_notes: DO Rueda: aroma and flavour with notes of scrubland herbs ('hierba de monte bajo'). Decanter: key aromas such as freshly cut grass, fennel and lime zest. SevenFifty Daily: 'lively, herbaceous wines'. Appellation rules: Verdejo gives Rueda whites their freshness ('frescura').

value: By far the dominant grape and the only one in a wine labelled Rías Baixas Albariño, which must be 100 percent Albariño. It also leads the subzone blends of Condado do Tea, Rosal and Salnés, which need at least 70 percent of their named main varieties.
source_notes: Appellation rules: Albariño by far the majority variety; Rías Baixas Albariño 100% Albariño; Condado do Tea >=70% Albariño and Treixadura, Rosal and Salnés >=70% of listed varieties incl. Albariño. Decanter: if the label says Albariño it must be 100% Albariño; Salnés effectively all Albariño, other subzones blend small shares of Treixadura, Loureiro, Caíño Blanco. Museo do Viño de Galicia (Xunta): same 100% and 70% rules.

value: Here the wines pair their fresh acidity with real structure and a gently creamy, lingering texture, valued more for acidity and aroma than for alcohol.
source_notes: Appellation rules: Rías Baixas Albariño has good structure, medium unctuousness and persistence; the climate gives wines known more for their acidity and aroma than their alcohol. Decanter: Rías Baixas Albariño is aromatic and mineral, structured and creamy, long and long lived.

value: Toro's principal red grape and the basis of its flagship reds.
source_notes: Appellation rules: 'Principal: Tinta de Toro', Garnacha Tinta secondary. Decanter (sponsored feature on DO Toro): 'the appellation's flagship Tinta de Toro reds'.

value: Here it makes more concentrated, powerful reds with firm, grippy tannins.
source_notes: Appellation rules: Tinta de Toro is 'más tánica', with 'vinos más concentrados y potentes'. Wine Folly: Toro makes a rich style known for 'robust, grippy tannins'. Decanter: greater flavour concentration and tannic structure than Tempranillo.

value: The defining white grape: a wine labelled Valdeorras Godello is made from Godello alone, and the sparkling wine needs at least 85 percent.
source_notes: Appellation rules: Valdeorras Godello made exclusively from Godello; sparkling at least 85% Godello. GuildSomm: Godello is now the defining grape for Valdeorras. Museo do Viño de Galicia: Valdeorras Godello 100% Godello, sparkling more than 85% Godello.

value: Here it gives full, rounded whites with a gently oily texture, kept fresh by good natural acidity.
source_notes: Appellation rules: Valdeorras Godello structured and unctuous, natural acidity makes it fresh and elegant, full wines with a long finish. Guía Peñín: tasty with excellent acidity and often a greasy texture; its Ribeira Sacra page calls Ribeira Sacra Godello fresher and less glyceric than Valdeorras.

value: Here it gives fruit driven reds with well defined, ripe red fruit aromas.
source_notes: Appellation rules: Valdeorras reds show intense aromas of ripe red fruit, medium to high acidity and balanced tannin. Guía Peñín: well defined fruity aromas, dry and fruity on the palate, Atlantic and Mediterranean character.
